title: One Piece Day returns to Tokyo Big Sight and worldwide on Youtube 22 and 23 August
description: A day so nice they made it twice. It’s beginning to look a lot like One Piece Day, everywhere you go. But it’s at Tokyo Big Sight to see the pirates that will be arriving aaaaaashore… Sorry, I just can’t help getting caught up in the spirit of One Piece Day and start singing One […]
content:
A day so nice they made it twice.

It’s beginning to look a lot like One Piece Day, everywhere you go. But it’s at Tokyo Big Sight to see the pirates that will be arriving aaaaaashore…

Sorry, I just can’t help getting caught up in the spirit of One Piece Day and start singing One Piece carols day and night. Yes, it’s that time of year again when Tokyo Big Sight becomes the center of all things One Piece, from manga and anime to video games and figures and everything in between. And as always, there’s just so much stuff that the day has to span two full days on 22 and 23 August.

The doors will open on 22 August, where fans can check out the latest in One Piece merchandise, along with some limited edition goods, as well as rare items and artwork from the franchise’s various productions. The day will come to a close with an Opening Day Panel featuring “We Are!” singer Hiroshi Kitadani, followed by a countdown of the first 70 of the World Top 100 character popularity poll.

The next day has a packed schedule of events such as panels with the musicians and voice actors behind One Piece and special announcements about the future of the series’ many iterations and adaptations, especially the trading card game. The top 30 of the World Top 100 will also be counted down, and the 8th annual One Piece Knowledge King finals will be held to crown the most knowledgeable fan around.

And of course, the highlight of any One Piece Day event is always the musical performances. This year, attendees will be treated to performances by Aina The End, who sings the current opening theme “Luminous,” and 36km/h, who made the ending theme “Future.”

And for those not in the Tokyo area, One Piece Day will also once again be livestreamed worldwide via the franchise’s official English YouTube channel, with English-speaking hosts and interviewers. It’s also possible to take part in the fun without being present at Tokyo Big Sight. For example, although voting has ended for the World Top 100, you can still go on the One Piece Base app and make your predictions for the top 30 characters. Correct predictions will be rewarded with special digital goodies on the app.

So, be sure to head on down, either virtually or in person, and join in the annual celebration of One Piece. I already have my One Piece Day decorations all set up.

title: Are Japan’s room-temperature curry packets the boxed lunch heroes we’ve been looking for? [Taste test]
description: Packets of curry you can store and eat at room temperature could be the answer to our prayers for portable, smell-safe curry. Curry and rice is always a winning combination, but the road to victory can be a difficult one when you’re packing a lunch to take with when you’re heading out for the day. […]
content:
Packets of curry you can store and eat at room temperature could be the answer to our prayers for portable, smell-safe curry.

Curry and rice is always a winning combination, but the road to victory can be a difficult one when you’re packing a lunch to take with when you’re heading out for the day. Curry rice might seem like it’d work great for a home-made bento boxed lunch, since it’s a dish you can eat out of a single container with just a spoon, but transporting curry comes with the risks of the roux, or its aroma, leaking out inside your bag, car, or elsewhere before you make it to lunchtime.

But it looks like we might have found a solution to this problem thanks to Miyajima Shoyu Co., a Tokyo-based maker of soy sauce and other condiments. Miyajima offers something they call the Hitokuchi Series, and it includes packets of ready-to-eat curry!

In addition to Hitokuchi Curry, there’s also Hitokuchi Stew and Hitokuchi Hayashi, packets of cream stew and hayashi rice sauce (similar to a tomato-based demi-glace sauce). For our taste test, we opted for a combo bundle with a total of 10 packets so that we could try all three.

▼ Hitokuchi Curry (yellow), Stew (white), and Hayashi (red)

The packets can be stored at room temperature and eaten without reheating, and they have a shelf life of over one year, so keeping a stock in your pantry, or carrying a few with you when travelling or camping, are viable options. The packets are easy to open without getting your hands messy, and the sufficiently thick consistency of the sauces means that they don’t come dribbling out and spilling in places you don’t want them to. That thickness also makes it easy to regulate the speed at which you squeeze them out, so there’s no worry of accidentally overflowing your plate or bento box because you put too much on your rice too quickly.

▼ Left to right: curry, stew, and hayashi

So how do they taste? Very nice, across the board. The curry is on the mild side, but Japanese curry is more about the overall combination of spices than just simple spiciness. Hitokuchi Curry fits with the familiar expectations for Japanese curry, and it’s a flavor that a wide range of people will be able to enjoy, and it was tasty even at room temperature.

The Hitokuchi Hayashi had a surprising amount of tomato tang to its flavor profile, but still balanced with enough sweetness to keep from feeling harsh, though it had the most impactful flavor of the three Hitokuchi siblings. Finally, the Hitokuchi Stew was satisfyingly creamy. We were a little worried about eating cream stew with rice, as it’s not a common combination in Japanese cooking, but it turned out that they can play nicely together, though we do have to admit that it felt a little unusual eating stew at room temperature since it’s usually served piping hot. But yeah, if the question is “Do they taste good?”, the Hitokuchi series goes three for three.

So as long as you’ve got a bento box of rice and a single Hitokuchi Curry packet, are you all set for lunch? Probably not. For one thing, each packet only contains 30 grams (about one ounce). Considering that Hitokuchi literally translates to “a single bite,” that modest quantity doesn’t mean that Hitokuchi Curry is falsely advertised, but it does mean that a single packet probably isn’t going to be enough for the amount of rice one would usually put in their bento. One packet is enough if you’re looking for a changeup in flavor as you finish off the last few mouthfuls of rice, but if you want enough curry to enjoy for the entire meal, you’re probably going to need three packets.

▼ This does, though, open up possibilities like the triple-temptation curry stew hayashi rice we made for ourselves.

On the other hand, one Hitokuchi packet is enough if you’re spreading it on some toast, which we can confirm is a tasty alternative.

The other thing to be aware of is that unlike some kinds of instant curry that toss in a few slices of vegetables or pieces of meat, the Hitokuchi series is strictly roux/sauce, so if there are any other toppings you want, you’re going to have to provide/procure them separately.

That said, in terms of what it promises to be, a mouthful of curry sauce in a packet, Hitokuchi Curry works very well. We found our curry/stew/hayashi bundle on Amazon Japan here for 1,340 yen, but if you’re all about the curry, a 10-pack of Hitokuchi Curry packets is also available here for 795 yen.

content:
Retro telephone from the Guchokipanya bakery plays one of the film’s most iconic songs.

Studio Ghibli movies are filled with intriguing characters that have the power to completely draw us into their animated worlds, and in Kiki’s Delivery Service, it’s Jiji who often steals the show.

Now, the black cat is back in the spotlight, thanks to a new release from Ghibli specialty retailer Donguri Kyowakoku. Called “Kiki’s Delivery Service Music Box: A Message to Kiki”, this music box is modeled after the black rotary telephone at Guchokipanya, the bakery where Kiki begins her new life.

The product is beautifully designed, with the phone receiver shown off the hook, propped up against the black telephone. With Jiji leaning in, ears perked towards the receiver, as if wondering who might be on the line, it’s almost as if we can hear the faint voice of someone, perhaps a customer, or maybe even Kiki herself, greeting us from a faraway location.

▼ Is that you, Kiki?

The sound that really comes out of the phone, however, is “Rouge no Dengon” (“Message of Rouge“), the iconic opening theme song from Kiki’s Delivery Service.

Both the music and the design of the music box itself evoke the warm, nostalgic feel of the bakery, right down to the delicate lace detailing on the wooden-look base.

▼ The phone cord is soft and malleable, just as it would be on a real rotary telephone.

Measuring approximately 10.5 × 13 × 10.5 centimetres (4.1 × 5.1 × 4.1 inches) and weighing around 532 grams (1.17 pounds), the music box looks like it’s jumped straight out of the anime world of Ghibli. Whether you’re enjoying it as a music box or a decorative display piece, this beautiful product is bound to put a smile on your face whenever you lay eyes on it, and it can be purchased at Donguri Kyowakoku stores in Japan and online from 10 a.m. on 8 August.

title: Tokyo is getting a branch of famous Los Angeles hot dog chain Pink’s with Japan-exclusive items
description: 87-year-old hot dog chain is going to learn some new tricks. content:
87-year-old hot dog chain is going to learn some new tricks.

It’s been about a year since Los Angeles’ iconic Randy’s Donuts opened its first branch in Japan, and as much as we love the place, even we have to admit that eating donuts every day for breakfast, lunch, and dinner probably wouldn’t be a very good idea. But for those looking to diversify looking to diversify their diet yet still craving something with ties to the City of Angels, now comes word that Pink’s is on its way to Japan.

Husband and wife Paul and Betty Pink started Pink’s Hot Dogs with a modest push cart on the streets of L.A. all the way back in 1939. Their big break came seven years later when they opened a permanent restaurant in the Fairfax District, close enough to Hollywood that Pink’s became a favorite of movie stars, show biz celebrities, and other people wanting to grab a bite to eat between visits to local nightlife hot spots.

Today, Pink’s has eight locations in southern California and two in the neighboring state of Nevada, and soon they’ll have their very first branch in Japan. Thanks to a partnership with Japanese restaurant management and consulting firm Sunpark, Pink’s plan is to be serving hot dogs in Tokyo by the end of this year.

Though specific menu details for Pink’s Japan have yet to be revealed, the announcement mentions the chain’s extensive variety toppings such as chili, cheese, bacon, jalapenos, and onion rings. In addition to hot dogs, the Japan branch will have hamburgers, desserts, and other side menu items, and it’s also promising Japan-exclusive items that are tailored to local tastes.

The exact location where Pink’s will open in Tokyo is also still under wraps, but the goal is for the chain to have 30 branches in Japan by the end of 2030.

title: Japanese convenience store food gets turned into hyper-realistic stationery you can peel open
description: The rice ball and hot snack sets let you feel the fun of some of Japan’s best treats anywhere in the world. content:
The rice ball and hot snack sets let you feel the fun of some of Japan’s best treats anywhere in the world.

Japan’s convenience stores are filled with wondrous foods to try, with new delights appearing regularly, but there is one staple that any visitor to Japan must try: the humble onigiri. These rice balls may look unassuming, but are the perfect treat to grab if you want a quick meal amid a busy schedule, sating those hungry-stomach rumblings. Releasing on September 18, Japanese stationery maker King Jim has decided to give onigiri a playful makeover in their new Jim Mart lineup, transforming everyday desk supplies into irresistible snacks that bring a spark of joy to your workspace.

Japanese convenience stores are famous for their quality, variety, and satisfying packaging, all of which is captured by the Jim Mart merchandise, giving you practical functionality and an authentic unboxing experience that includes the peel-and-tear pull tabs found on rice ball packets.

Designed just like the famous triangular rice balls, the Onigiri Erasers and Onigiri Clips come wrapped in realistic pull-strip packaging, which when peeled reveals a reusable rice-ball-shaped case housing your erasers or clips. Fillings include red salmon, plum, tuna and mayonnaise, and raw cod roe, with each pack containing two varieties, three pieces each.

▼ Both erasers and clips cost 650 yen (US$4.10), excluding tax.

Available in eight total varieties split across triangular and round rice ball shapes, these Onigiri Letters come with clear, perforated outer envelopes, granting the recipient the enjoyment of peeling open a fresh convenience snack to read your message, complete with address stickers styled after authentic package labels. Each set contains two cards, envelopes, and stickers.

▼ All onigiri letter varieties cost 540 yen.

Inspired by the hot treats found right by the register, these Hot Snack Card and Envelope Sets come in four tasty styles: fried chicken, corn dog, karaage (Japanese fried chicken), and French fries. The envelope designs mimic real hot snack bags, complete with tear-away perforations or flap closures, and include store-style sealing stickers.

▼ Hot Snack Sets cost 540 yen, excluding tax.

With Japanese convenience stores having become a must-visit destination for international travelers, and the impracticality of carting home easily perishable items, the Jim Mart collection also doubles as the ultimate gift or souvenir. The whole lineup can be ordered through the King Jim online store here.

Whether you are looking to brighten up your study desk, surprise a stationery-loving friend, or take home a piece of Japanese culture, this deliciously fun series is one to take a look at, but try your best to wrestle down your appetite as you’re writing your friend a message.

description: Kumamoto City izakaya began flooding with hot, sulfur-smelling water immediately after quake. content:
Kumamoto City izakaya began flooding with hot, sulfur-smelling water immediately after quake.

The earthquake that occurred in Kumamoto Prefecture on July 28 caused extensive damage to the region, and among those affected was Mugi Usagi, an restaurant in the Anseimachi neighborhood of Kumamoto City’s Chuo Ward. Mugu Usagi is an izakaya, a kind of Japanese pub specializing in small dishes meant to be paired with beer, sake, or cocktails, but it looks like the location might have one more desirous commodity, as apparently the restaurant’s building sits on top of a previously undiscovered hot spring.

Shortly after the earthquake hit, water began flooding the restaurant’s interior. The source of liquid, though, wasn’t a broken water pipe, as it was instead coming up through the floor of the restaurant’s storeroom.

▼ The flooded Mugi Usagi can be seen at the point queued in the video below.

The water was hot to the touch, so much so that steam began to fill the room. Again, though, the water wasn’t coming from a buster pipe or water heater, and what’s more, it had a distinctly sulfurous aroma, and after repair workers came in to survey the damage, they informed the restaurant’s owner that it was likely hot spring water that was flooding the place.

Even with as much as Japan loves a nice hot bath, there are still hot springs in the country that have remained hidden for many years. Currently, Mugi Usagi’s ownership is focused on repairing the restaurant and getting back to serving diners and drinkers, but with the proven popularity of bathhouses in urban areas, it wouldn’t be a surprise if someone is looking into whether it’d be viable to add one to the building.

title: This beautiful rural Japan river is a great alternative to touristy summer retreats [Photos]
description: The Enbaragawa River’s lighting and subsurface flow put it on a different level of natural beauty. In Japan, the summer heat can be sweltering, intense, or even downright cruel. What it’s not, though, is inescapable. For generations, one way of coping with hot weather has been to head up into the mountains, where temperatures are cooler […]
content:
The Enbaragawa River’s lighting and subsurface flow put it on a different level of natural beauty.

In Japan, the summer heat can be sweltering, intense, or even downright cruel. What it’s not, though, is inescapable. For generations, one way of coping with hot weather has been to head up into the mountains, where temperatures are cooler than in the cities and coastal areas. However, if you head to such famous summer retreats as, say, Karuizawa in Nagano Prefecture, you’re going to be trying to run away from the heat by running right into huge tourist crowds.

So the trick is to find someplace cool and relaxing, but not quite so touristy, and that brings us to the Enbaragawa River in the mountains of Gifu Prefecture.

Enbaragawa isn’t exactly a “hidden gem,” as it attracts visitors from outside Gifu too. As the same time, it’s not nearly as congested as Japan’s more prominent beat-the-heat travel destinations. The best section of the river to visit is located in Gifu’s Yamagata City, and it’s far enough off the beaten path that phone service gets kind of spotty, so you’ll want to sort out your driving route while you’re still someplace where you have a signal.

▼ The sport we’ll be heading to in this article

▼ 円原川 = Enbaragawa

▼ There’s a covered free parking area located along the road immediately south of the pin in the map above.

There are signs guiding visitors down to the riverbank…

…and once you do get down there, the scenery is dazzling, sometimes literally so.

In this section of the river, mist coming off the water regularly mingles with the sunlight filtered through the tree branches overhead, creating radiant photo opportunities. The best times to see/photograph this phenomenon are in July and August between 7:30 and 9 a.m., with peak picturesqueness at about 8 o’clock, but even if you show up a little later in the day, like we did, you can still see some great views.

The water itself is also incredibly beautiful. Enbaragawa is a subsurface-flow river, meaning that for a portion of the waterway, the water flows underground. In Enbaragawa’s case, the water flows for about two kilometers (1.2 miles) through a section of limestone bedrock which helps filter out impurities, resulting in amazing clarity.

Between the lighting, the clear water, and the moss-covered stones, everywhere we turned our camera looked like a scene from a movie or the cover of a travel guide, and even just sitting by the side of the stream, taking in the sights and sounds, felt luxuriously soothing.

Ah, but we’re here to beat the heat, right? Sitting in the shade at Enbaragawa it was cool enough to make us forget that it was actually a fiercely hot day for so much of the country, but we wanted to feel even cooler, so it was time to dip our toes in the water…

…and once we got used to the invigorating chill, to wade out deeper.

Splashing around and scampering over the rocks is sure to trigger thoughts of nostalgic visits to Grandma and Grandpa’s place in the Japanese countryside during summer vacation (even if that wasn’t actually a part of your childhood).

While the river isn’t really deep enough here for full-on swimming for adults, there is enough depth to get your clothes pretty soaked, so you might want to bring something to change into if you don’t want to wait for your outfit to air-dry.

We spotted a few visitors reading or napping in the shade of the riverside trees, but there’s another activity waiting for when you’re ready to get out of the river. Head south along the road until you get to the point marked here…

…and you’ll see the Enbara River Steel Bridge.

Accessing the bridge actually requires you to walk along a path through a bit of private land, which the owner graciously allows passage through, so please take care not to leave any trash behind or make too much noise.

The bridge isn’t incredibly high, but with no guard rails on either side, it can be a little unnerving to take the first few steps.

It’s worth pushing through the apprehension, though, in order to enjoy the special vantage point.

Standing by the stream, with the gentle burbling of the water the only sound we could hear, may not have been a flashy form of entertainment, but it was deeply relaxing and rewarding, and we’ll have to keep Enbaragawa in mind for the next time we need to get away from the hustle, bustle, and heat of daily life.

Reference: Gifu Travel Guide

title: Japan’s new beer glass is designed to force you to drink…water [Video]
description: Yona Yona has a furatsuku idea to promote responsible drinking. One of the cruelest twists of fate is that on a hot afternoon few things feel more refreshing than an ice-cold beer, and yet beer, as an alcoholic beverage, does a poor job of keeping your body hydrated. Yeah, that first cold one might feel […]
content:
Yona Yona has a furatsuku idea to promote responsible drinking.

One of the cruelest twists of fate is that on a hot afternoon few things feel more refreshing than an ice-cold beer, and yet beer, as an alcoholic beverage, does a poor job of keeping your body hydrated. Yeah, that first cold one might feel rejuvenating, but keep knocking back one beer after another, and they’re going to take a toll on you later on.

Of course, just like it’s not very helpful for hydration, beer isn’t all that good for boosting willpower or memory retention either. So should you find yourself needing a little outside help remembering to maintain a moderate pace and proper non-beer fluid intake levels, Japanese beer brand Yona Yona Ale has something for you.

They call it the Furatsuku (“wobbly” or “staggering”) Beer Glass, and while it might at first look like it’s half-empty in the photo above, that’s not what’s happening, and no, we don’t mean that in an optimistic “It’s actually half-full” kind of way. Those Furatsuku Beer Glasses being clinked together are both full, with no halves about it, because there’s a divider at the bottom that separates each of them into two sections.

You fill one section with beer, and the other with water, and as long as the amounts of liquid in the two parts are more or less equal, the glass won’t tip over. However, should you keep chugging away at the beer only without sipping any of the water, the center of balance will shift, and the glass will topple over and spill.

Ah, but what if you’re so fond of barley-based beverages that you weren’t planning on setting your glass down at all? It looks like the Furatsuku Beer Glass will still make sure you drink some water. As you tilt the glass further back to drain one section, the opposite rim also starts angling towards you. Drink too much beer without taking a water break, and you’ll end up with water cascading directly onto your forehead.

Technically, this means that the vessel won’t let you drink too much water without also having some beer, but considering that it’s called the Furatsuku Beer Glass, we can take it as a given that anyone using it had already decided to have some beer.

As of August 5, the Furatsuku Beer Glass is being offered as an option to customers at Yona Yona Beer Works pub in downtown Tokyo’s Shinbashi neighborhood, but for those who’d like one for their home, it’s also available for purchase through the Yona Yona online store here, priced at 13,750 yen (US$88), with shipping scheduled for mid-September. Until then, we’ll just have to drink from the other strange but clever glass that Yona Yona designed.

title: This Japanese chopping board sanitising bag might be the handy kitchen gadget we never knew we needed
description: We find out if a bag made specifically for soaking chopping boards is actually useful. How do you disinfect your chopping boards? If your answer to that question is “With great difficulty” or “Huh? We’re meant to disinfect chopping boards?” then we would like to introduce you to… ▼ … the Chopping Board Sanitising Bag. […]
content:
We find out if a bag made specifically for soaking chopping boards is actually useful.

How do you disinfect your chopping boards? If your answer to that question is “With great difficulty” or “Huh? We’re meant to disinfect chopping boards?” then we would like to introduce you to…

▼ … the Chopping Board Sanitising Bag.

The idea is simple: put your chopping board inside, then add water and detergent, or diluted chlorine-based kitchen bleach, which is commonly used in Japan to disinfect chopping boards.

▼ The bag (袋) comes with an Any Lock (エニーロック) sealing clip and a funnel (じょうご) for pouring in liquids.

The bag is designed so the chopping board can be fully submerged while floating inside, with the airtight seal helping to prevent any cleaning-agent odours from escaping.


When we tried it out, we were happy to find that the medium-large size that we’d ordered easily fit our large 37 × 22 cm (14.6 × 8.7 inches) chopping board. Alternatively, it’s roomy enough to fit two medium-sized chopping boards.

▼ After sealing the opening securely with the Any Lock clip…

▼ … the centre flap lifted slightly, making it easy to pour the cleaning detergent in using the funnel.

We ended up using around 600 millilitres of liquid to fully submerge the board. Because the bag is sealed shut, oxygen-based bleach should not be used.

Once the soaking is complete, simply pour the liquid out by sliding the Any Lock clip halfway open.


To dry the bag, simply hang it up with a peg. The inside can take a little longer to dry, so if you place something sturdy like a chopstick inside to keep the bag open, it helps to speed up the drying process.

▼ When not in use, the bag can be folded away for compact storage.


After using the product, we found it had some pros and cons. Starting with the pros, the biggest advantage is that you can soak both sides of the chopping board, as well as the edges, evenly in one go. Not having to repeatedly change the water or flip the board over made things much easier than expected.

If you have small children or pets, the product is particularly useful as you don’t have to worry about them accidentally touching the detergent solution if you were cleaning it in a filled sink, for example. The securely sealed bag gives you extra peace of mind. The main downside, though, is that you can’t put it away until the inside has completely dried, so be prepared for it to lie around taking up space for a while after you use it.

So can you live without this sanitising bag? Well, yes, but you can also live without sanitising your chopping boards too. If you do like to err on the side of caution by disinfecting your boards as many recommend doing, then this is a surprisingly useful little kitchen helper. The M-L size has a recommended retail price of 1,100 yen (US$6.76), and it can be purchased at Iwatani retailers and online shopping sites like Amazon and Rakuten.

title: Tired of city life? Try out Japanese rural life for a few days on an active volcano in Kagoshima
description: Escape Tokyo to harvest mandarins, dig footbaths, or learn how to run an inn. Many people have dreams of where they would like to live, and it can sometimes be starkly different from the environment in which they have grown up, but there are few who truly decide to take the plunge. content:
Escape Tokyo to harvest mandarins, dig footbaths, or learn how to run an inn.

Many people have dreams of where they would like to live, and it can sometimes be starkly different from the environment in which they have grown up, but there are few who truly decide to take the plunge. Trading the hustle and bustle of city life for a peaceful rural retreat sounds like an idyllic lifestyle, although it’s difficult to make that leap without trying it first. Kagoshima City has now partnered, though, with All Nippon Airways (ANA) and ANA Akindo (a company focused on airline sales and marketing, and regional revitalization) and created the perfect opportunity for you to do just that, launching a trial migration program designed to give participants a genuine taste of life in rural Japan.

▼ Scenery in the rural area of Yoshida

Targeted at young adults under 40 and families with children residing in major metropolitan areas like Tokyo, Nagoya, or Osaka, this initiative serves as a welcoming bridge to dual-region living. Whether you are an international resident exploring possible options beyond the major cities or you’re simply eager to experience authentic Japanese culture, this program connects you to local communities through hands-on activities, cultural immersion, and outdoor adventures.

You can choose from several tailored multi-day itineraries across two areas: Yoshida, which is focused on the countryside and family life, and Sakurajima, centered on volcano and island life.

The Parent-Child Discovery program in the tranquil Yoshida area lasts for three days and two nights, where groups or families of four people can experience rural living surrounded by hot springs and starry skies. They can also look forward to farm harvesting, local craft-making (such as making miso and woodworking), and visits to local schools.

▼ Harvesting vegetables

▼ Making miso

Applications for programs in Yoshida are being accepted from now until September 30 for stays starting between mid-October 2026 and mid-January 2027. Activity materials will cost 2,000 yen (US$12.70) per person, and participants are required to cover their own accommodation, food, and local transport costs.

Meanwhile, on the volcanic island of Sakurajima, prospective participants have the choice of four different programs to get involved in: Daily Life, Volcanic Activities, Seasonal Harvest Experience, and Guest House Open Bootcamp.

The Daily Life experience is for people looking to stay in local guest houses for at least four days, harvesting produce, cycling, and discovering what it’s like to live on a volcano that’s almost constantly smoking. Recruitment is from now through January 31 for stays between October 1 and February 28, with the total plan cost ranging from 6,600 yen to 23,100 yen per person, covering lodging and activities, although meals and local transport are extra.

▼ Harvesting giant Japanese radishes

The Volcanic Activities program lasts for at least four days, where participants can dive into nature with trekking, freediving, footbath digging, and pottery. Recruitment is from now to November 30 for stays between October 1 and December 24. The total cost for the program is 9,900-23,100 per person, covering both lodging and activities, whereas meals and local transport are extra.

▼ Freediving

▼ Digging a footbath

The Seasonal Harvest Experience allows you to work with local farmers for four or more days, picking famous Sakurajima mandarins and giant radishes. Applications are accepted between now and December 31 for stays between December 1 and January 31. The total costs are 13,200-19,800 yen per person, including the lodging and harvest activities, but meals and local transport are extra.

The final Guest House Open Bootcamp is targeted at prospective entrepreneurs who might be considering starting a business or managing guest houses on Sakurajima. Participants will spend three days learning how to revitalize abandoned and empty houses, repurposing them, giving them new life. The application period is from now to December 31 for a fixed stay period of February 21 to February 23. The total cost is between 36,600-43,200 per person, which includes the two-night stay plus a 30,000-yen seminar and networking fee, with meals and local transport extra.

▼ You can observe working guesthouses

For stays on Sakurajima, you’ll be spending the night at one of the local guest houses, depending on which program you’re on. Participants in all of the programs can stay at the Iko Terrace or Ulala Furusato.

▼ Iko Terrace

For the Guest House Open Bootcamp, there is one more option, Umino Terrace.

▼ Umino Terrace

While anyone joining the programs is expected to pay their own way there, they do receive some round-trip airfare support via ANA Sky Coins, equivalent to 20,000 yen in credit for flights from Tokyo and Nagoya, or 15,000 yen from Osaka. All you need to do is reserve your flights on the ANA website and apply the digital coins toward your fare, paying any remaining balance out-of-pocket.

For anyone interested in any of the programs, you just need to complete the free registration on ANA’s official portal site, with profile approval typically taking three to five business days. You will be expected to participate in the chosen local activities, and complete a post-trip feedback session with local staff to help shape future regional initiatives. However, they do give a warning that canceling after your participation is confirmed will incur a cancellation fee equivalent to the amount of ANA Sky Coins granted, so choose your dates carefully.

If you’re ready to see whether country living is your true calling, head over to the portal site and take the first step toward your Kagoshima adventure. Even if you don’t see yourself settling down there, the prefecture is filled with hidden gems that are definitely worth exploring.

title: Bandai looking to introduce Japanese government ID checks for admission to card game events
description: Don’t have a My Number Card from the Japanese government? You might not be getting into some events for One Piece or other Bandai trading card games. Recently, the Pokémon Company announced a new system that requires proof of identity through a Japanese government-issued ID card to purchase certain Pokémon Card Game items or participate […]
content:
Don’t have a My Number Card from the Japanese government? You might not be getting into some events for One Piece or other Bandai trading card games.

Recently, the Pokémon Company announced a new system that requires proof of identity through a Japanese government-issued ID card to purchase certain Pokémon Card Game items or participate in selected events. It turns out they’re not the only otaku-oriented company that likes the idea of having you verify your identity with the backing of the Japanese government, as Bandai has announced that it’s looking to introduce a similar requirement starting as early as next month.

The announcement was made through the official Twitter account of Bandai Card Games, the division of Bandai that manages collectible trading card games based on the One Piece, Dragon Ball, Naruto, Gundam, and Digimon franchises, as well as the anime crossover card game Union Arena.

【BANDAI TCG+に関する重要なお知らせ】

すべてのお客様に公平な機会を提供し、より安心・安全にサービスをご利用いただけるよう、「マイナンバーカード」を用いた本人確認システムの導入を検討しております。… pic.twitter.com/1c0Xu3qNrr

— 【OFFICIAL】BANDAI CARD GAMES (@official_BCG_JP) August 5, 2026

“In order to provide equal opportunities and a safe, secure service to all customers, we are investigating the idea of introducing an ID verification system utilizing the My Number Card,” says the statement, referring to the combination ID/national pension/national health insurance card issued by the Japanese government.

In addition to the bearer’s name and photo, the My Number Card also lists their home address and date of birth. While that same information can be found on many forms of identification, the system that Bandai Card Games is describing would specifically require verification through the My Number Card, not an alternate class of ID such as a driver’s license or student ID card.

All residents of Japan aged 15 or older, including foreign residents, are eligible for a My Number Card, but that also means that any system which requires the card to be presented effectively locks out any tourists in Japan. In addition, not all residents have applied for a My Number Card, with many having concerns about privacy or the security of the government’s data handling/storage protocols.

The Bandai Card Games announcement doesn’t appear to offer much hope for those looking for an alternative, though, as is says “For those without a My Number Card, we recommend applying for one as soon as possible, as the process of issuing the card can take a certain amount of time.”

Bandai Card Games says that is progressing with preparations to have a My Number verification requirement in place sometime around September of this year. As for the extent of the requirement, right now the company is saying that it will be used for ID verification for admission to selected Bandai Card Games events, but also that is looking into applying the system for other purposes farther in the future, ostensibly requiring My Number Card verification for eligibility to purchase certain items. This would be in keeping with the recently increased efforts to discourage scalpers from bulk buying products for the purpose of reselling them at inflated prices, as the My Number Card would help identify and block individuals buying abnormally large quantities that are clearly beyond a reasonable amount for personal use.

All else equal, I think we can agree that most genuine fans of a game or series would be happy to see speculative scalpers’ money-grubbing schemes shut down. As for foreign tourists being shut out of certain events, many official card game competitions already have local residency as a registration requirement, and language differences mean that most overseas fans aren’t looking to buy cards in Japan since they’re printed in Japanese, making them hard to play with back in their home countries. However, much like with the Pokémon Company’s new policy, the unsettling part of Bandai introducing a My Number Card verification system is the possibility that it could expand its scope beyond trading card games to encompass other, non-card game items in its vast anime merchandising empire, though thankfully that hasn’t come to pass yet.

title: New Japanese vending machine at Shinkansen station sells cups of ice on platform
description: A new way to make your journey on Japan’s fastest trains even cooler. content:
A new way to make your journey on Japan’s fastest trains even cooler.

If you’re about to take a bullet train ride on a hot summer day, you’ll be happy to know that Central Japan Railway Company has just installed a new station platform vending machine selling something cold and refreshing. However, this machine doesn’t sell cans of cola, bottles of tea, or even tubs of ice cream. Instead, it sells cups of ice.

As of August 7, travelers passing through Shin Osaka Station on the Tokaido Shinkansen line (which connects Osaka, Kyoto, and Tokyo) will find a Fuji Electric FFS107WFXU1 vending machine on Platform 27. Ordinarily this model is used to store and sell frozen foods, but the Shinkansen platform one is stocked entirely with Rock Ice Glass, containers of ice cubes.

Though crunching into the cubes as an edible snack is, technically, an option, that’s not really their intended use. As fast as the Shinkansen may be, it still takes about two and a half hours to get from Osaka to Tokyo by bullet train, and roughly the same amount of time for the trip from Osaka to Fukuoka, so any beverage you’re taking onboard with you is going to get lukewarm long before you reach your destination. The new vending machine gives travelers a way to keep a separately purchased drink cold for an extended period of time by pouring it into the Rock Ice Glass after they’re seated on the train.

Of course, there are limits to how long the ice will last before it melts. Rock Ice Glass has already proven to be a big seller at stores and kiosks within Shin Osaka Station, though, so there’s clearly a demand for it among rail travelers, and by placing the vending machine right on the Shinkansen platform, passengers can get theirs just before boarding, so that they’ll have the maximum amount of time to use it during their ride.

▼ Despite the name. Rock Ice Glass comes in a plastic cup.

The Rock Ice Glass vending machine is located on Platform 27 near where Car 6 of incoming Shinkansen trains stops. Payment is by cashless (IC transit card or bar code) methods only, and at 220 yen (US$1.40) it might be slightly more expensive than the drink you’re pouring into it, but it’s hard to put a price on the pleasure of an ice-cold drink during a Japanese summer, especially since the Shinkansen no longer sells beverages onboard.

title: Japanese toilet aims to attract foreign tourists but not everybody is happy about it
description: Rural town’s attempt to draw tourists may have gone a step too far. In recent years, Japanese public toilets have become known not only as places to do your business but as tourist attractions with creative design features. So you can’t really blame the Kagawa Prefectural Government when they saw an opportunity to turn a […]
content:
Rural town’s attempt to draw tourists may have gone a step too far.

In recent years, Japanese public toilets have become known not only as places to do your business but as tourist attractions with creative design features. So you can’t really blame the Kagawa Prefectural Government when they saw an opportunity to turn a local public toilet into a tourist magnet. However, the resulting facility turned out to be so extravagant that it became a source of division instead.

The new building was unveiled to the public on 22 March outside JR Kinashi Station in Takamatsu, Kagawa Prefecture. During the official opening ceremony at the site that night, the mood was high, with government officials hailing it as a much-needed improvement to the previous outdated building, which housed a unisex, squat-style pit toilet that had long elicited complaints from residents over its poor condition and hygiene.

▼ This report shows the opening ceremony and the state of the former facilities.

When the station’s operators, JR Shikoku, said it would prefer to remove the facility altogether rather than rebuild it due to a lack of funds, prefectural officials stepped in with a plan to build a new public toilet, in order to serve the station’s approximately 600 daily boarding passengers, as well as students from a nearby prefectural high school who often stop to use the facilities.

▼ Kinashi Station sits two stops west of Takamatsu Station on the JR Yosan Line and ranks 14th out of Kagawa Prefecture’s 48 JR stations by passenger numbers.

The new building now contains separate men’s, women’s, and multi-purpose toilets with modern amenities, which locals have expressed appreciation for. The real wow factor, though, is the exterior, which acts as a canvas for two nightly projection mapping shows, held from 7:15 p.m. to 8:00 p.m. and again from 8:20 p.m. to 9:00 p.m. Weekday displays feature illuminated angel wings, while weekends showcase a rotating selection of different artworks, including student-produced videos.

While the light display has turned the public toilet into an eye-catching landmark, it also aims to help nurture young creators, with local students and emerging artists encouraged to submit their own projection mapping designs, giving them a rare opportunity to see their work displayed publicly.

Officials also hope the unusual attraction will encourage more visitors to stop by the area. As Japan’s leading producer of pine bonsai, Kinashi already attracts international visitors interested in the local craft, so it’s hoped that word of the unique building will spread amongst overseas travellers, helping to bring more tourism to the area.

Despite these admirable goals, the unusual concept has been attracting the wrong kind of attention, as many locals have been surprised to learn that the entire project reportedly cost around 100 million yen (US$670,000).

Local opinion over the cost has been divided, with some residents arguing that the money could have been better spent elsewhere, while others say the discussion itself has helped to shine a spotlight on the town and its attractions.

Like any revitalisation project, the return on investment may take some time to reveal itself, so we’ll have to wait and see whether this expensive toilet has the power to breathe new life into the town. One thing is certain, though – it’s certainly helped put Kinashi Station on the map by making headlines, and if you’d like to help support the town, you now know where to stop and do your business.

title: End of a manga era as Weekly Shonen Jump’s circulation drops under one million
description: Weekly Shonen Jump is still the biggest magazine in Japan, but its print circulation is getting smaller and smaller. For decades, the jewel in the crown of the manga magazine world has been Weekly Shonen Jump. However, these days the jewel isn’t shining nearly as brightly as it used to, with the latest statistics showing […]
content:
Weekly Shonen Jump is still the biggest magazine in Japan, but its print circulation is getting smaller and smaller.

For decades, the jewel in the crown of the manga magazine world has been Weekly Shonen Jump. However, these days the jewel isn’t shining nearly as brightly as it used to, with the latest statistics showing that publisher Shueisha’s anthology has crossed over a significant threshold.

The Japan Magazine Publishers Association has released circulation data for the first quarter of the Japanese business year (April to June). During that time, Weekly Shonen Jump’s average print circulation fell to 985,000 copies per week. Not only was that a 1.9-percent drop compared to the preceding three-month period, it’s the first time since 2008 for Weekly Shonen Jump’s circulation to slip below one million, and possibly even longer since that’s as far back as regularly publicized circulation for the magazine goes.

The magazine’s weekly circulation peaked in late 1994 at a towering 6.53 million copies, which is an all-time high not only for Weekly Shonen Jump itself but for any manga anthology in the industry. At the time, it was the home of both Dragon Ball and Slam Dunk, iconic hit series with extremely broad fan bases whose creators were pumping out new chapters every week. By 2017 circulation dipped under two million, though, and just under a decade later, it’s roughly half of that.

Weekly Shonen Jump’s is still, however, the biggest manga magazine in Japan, and by a large margin. Its closest rival is publisher Kodansha’s Weekly Shonen Magazine, which has an average circulation of 281,000 copies for the most recent period. Next comes Shueisha’s own Weekly Young Jump (aimed at older readers in the seinen demographic) at 214,000 and just behind it is Shogakukan’s Monthly CoroCoro Comic, with 213,333. Circulation for Shogakukan’s biggest weekly manga anthology, Weekly Shonen Sunday, is 120,000. Meanwhile, in the shojo manga demographic aimed at young girls, no magazine has a six-figure circulation, with Shueisha’s monthly Ribon’s 90,000 copies being the highest. Average circulation dropped for almost all of these publications in the most recent period, with the exceptions of Weekly Shonen Sunday, whose numbers were unchanged, and Monthly CoroCoro Comic, with an increase of 1.6 percent.

▼ Ribon

Weekly Shonen Jump also remains the highest-circulation print magazine, of any type, in Japan, but that status also means that Japan no longer has any magazines with a circulation of a million copies.

Weekly Shonen Jump’s dwindling circulation doesn’t mean that Shueisha, or the manga creators whose series the company serializes, are on the ropes, however. A big part of why demand for the print version of the anthology is dropping is because Japanese manga publishers and consumers alike have enthusiastically embraced digital distribution platforms. Circulation falling below one million isn’t so much a sign that people have lost interest in manga as it is that people are very interested in reading manga on their phones or other devices, and the convenience of being able to read manga digitally is undeniably a benefit to people living in neighborhoods where they don’t have easy access to a brick-and-mortar retailer or people who are too busy to make manga shopping runs on a weekly basis.

On the other hand, a strong digital shift has a negative effect on retailers who sell print manga, and while convenience stores and train station kiosks can rely on revenue from other products, the paper manga fading away is going to hit bookstores hard.

Some have also voiced concerns about whether digital publishing can make it harder for readers to discover new series. With a printed magazine, there’s a mindset that since you’ve paid for the issue, you may as well take a look at every series inside, even ones you haven’t heard of or read before, and doing so is as quick and easy as flipping a page. The vaster variety of titles within a digital manga app presents a greater threat of choice paralysis, where a reader is overwhelmed with options and so falls back on a familiar favorite rather than giving something new a shot, so manga’s increasingly digital future might require a bit more conscious effort on readers’ part to dive into a chapter of something they’ve never read before.

Source: Japan Magazine Publishers Association (1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7), TBS News Dig via Livedoor News, Yomiuri Shimbun

title: Studio Ghibli unveils new finger puppets featuring anime characters from My Neighbour Totoro
description: Recreate magical movie moments with beloved characters on your fingertips. When you become an adult you don’t always have to give up your childlike sense of fun and adventure, and Studio Ghibli is here to remind us of that fact with a new range of beautifully designed finger puppets. Called My Neighbour Totoro Soft Vinyl […]
content:
Recreate magical movie moments with beloved characters on your fingertips.

When you become an adult you don’t always have to give up your childlike sense of fun and adventure, and Studio Ghibli is here to remind us of that fact with a new range of beautifully designed finger puppets.

Called My Neighbour Totoro Soft Vinyl Mascot Finger Puppets, this collection consists of 11 different puppets, starring eight characters from My Neighbour Totoro.

Released by Ghibli specialty retailer Donguri Kyowakoku, the collection is the newest addition to the chain’s popular Sofubi Mascot Finger Puppet series, with “Sofubi” (ソフビ) used to mean “soft vinyl”.

Each puppet measures approximately 3.8 × 4.9 × 2.2 centimetres (1.5 × 1.9 × 0.9 inches) and weighs just 12 grams (0.4 ounces), making them light and easy to use for both adults and children.

Taking a closer look at the range, we have two sets dedicated to the titular character and the smaller of its species.

▼ They’re as cute from behind as they are from the front.

▼ Large Totoro

▼ Medium Totoro

▼ Small Totoro

The second set of Totoros recalls the magical night scene where they can be seen blowing into their musical ocarinas.

▼ Large Totoro Ocarina

▼ Medium Totoro Ocarina

▼ Small Totoro Ocarina

No collection from My Neighbour Totoro would truly be complete without an appearance from two members of the supporting cast, who are beautifully captured in miniature form.

▼ The Catbus…

▼ …and the Soot Sprites.

Rounding out the collection are three members from the human cast.

▼ Satsuki…

▼ … Kanta…

▼ … and Mei.

While all the characters above are ready to play out imaginative scenarios from the tips of your fingers, they’re so well sculpted that they make equally beautiful decorations.

Sure, the size discrepancies might mean that Mei has a harder time swatting the Soot Sprites between the palms of her hands…

▼… and the way she towers over the Catbus has it looking more like the Kittenbus…

▼ … but all these quirks can be reconciled with a little twist of the imagination.

A range this cute is likely to sell out fast, especially as each character puppet is reasonably priced at 770 yen (US$4.86). So be sure to hunt them down at your nearest branch of Donguri Kyowakoku in Japan, or keep your finger poised and ready to hit the purchase button when sales commence online at 10 a.m. on 8 August.

title: Anime fan in Japan arrested for ordering and cancelling over 4.3 billion yen in anime merch
description: Shop ‘till you drop unfortunately becomes shop ‘till you get arrested. As any hard-core fan can tell you, anime and manga can be a pricey hobby. Sure, the proliferation of video streaming services and digital reader apps mean the content itself is much more affordable than it used to be, but the modern otaku merchandising […]
content:
Shop ‘till you drop unfortunately becomes shop ‘till you get arrested.

As any hard-core fan can tell you, anime and manga can be a pricey hobby. Sure, the proliferation of video streaming services and digital reader apps mean the content itself is much more affordable than it used to be, but the modern otaku merchandising industry is more robust than ever, with an endless flow of figures, plushies, character standees, and more for fans to covet.

This brings us to a 32-year-old restaurant worker living in Osaka’s Kita Ward, who, in a statement to the police, said “I like anime,” and has the numerical data to back it up. Over a roughly two-year period beginning around October of 2023, she ordered more than 4.3 billion yen (US$27 million) worth of items from manga publisher Shueisha’s Jump Character Store. If you’re wondering how she managed to pay for all that merch on what’s assumedly a modest food service worker’s salary, the answer is that she didn’t.

That’s not to say that the woman, Mayu Yoshida, stole anything. Instead, she placed the orders but never paid for, or took delivery of, the items. She did this through two methods, the first of which involved exploiting Japan’s convenience store prepayment system. For shoppers who either don’t have a credit card or don’t want to carry a balance on it, many online retailers in Japan allow customers to place an order but pay for it at a convenience store, with the seller shipping the item once payment has been confirmed. There’s a limit, though, to how much time is allowed to pass between the order’s placement and payment, after which the order will be cancelled. So Yoshida would order figures, key chains, and other items through the Jump Character Shop, select the convenience store prepayment method, and just never actually go to pay for them. Between 2024 and 2025, she placed orders with a total bill of over 4.3 billion yen this way.

Her second strategy was to order items from the Jump Character Shop and select the cash-on-delivery payment method, wherein the recipient renders payment to the delivery person. In these instances, Yoshida would refuse delivery, and therefore not pay for, the things she’d ordered. It’s unclear what the total value was for the orders she refused delivery of, but you have to wonder if any delivery person got tired of coming to her house again and again.

▼ Please, ma’am, I’m begging you, pay for this one.

As a major online retailer, the Jump Character Store likely has protocols in place to flag orders from shoppers who habitually cancel or refuse delivery of their orders, but Yoshida got around these safeguards by creating 238 different customer accounts and hopping from one to another.

However, just because she wasn’t keeping any of the items without paying for them doesn’t make this a no-harm, no-foul situation. By not paying for the COD items, she also wasn’t paying for the shipping charges, leaving Shueisha with a cumulative bill of approximately 7.5 million yen in fees for items sent to her which then had to be returned. There’re also restocking and order-processing costs involved, all of which were enough for the police to arrest Yoshida on charges of fraudulent obstruction of business, which she has admitted to, on August 4.

The repeated targeting of the Jump Character Store might make it seem like she has a bone to pick with the manga magazine or its publisher, but that’s actually not the case. “I have been feeling stressed from daily life, and I felt a sense of satisfaction and refreshment from ordering items before they sold out,” said Yoshida following her arrest. “I do not have any resentment towards Shueisha.”

A particularly bittersweet aspect to the situation is that Yoshida had previously been a legitimate paying customer with the Jump Character Store, placing her first order in the fall of 2018. Hopefully once her legal situation is sorted out she’ll be able to return to a more responsible form of fandom.

title: 7-Eleven Japan rethinks convenience store drinks with new Grilled Corn Chilled Soup Smoothie
description: Exclusive to only two wards in Tokyo, this is a must-try drink that’s very hard to get. We’re always on the lookout for new and unusual convenience store finds in Japan, so when 7-Eleven announced it would be releasing a never-before-seen chilled soup smoothie made with grilled corn, we knew it was something we had […]
content:
Exclusive to only two wards in Tokyo, this is a must-try drink that’s very hard to get.

We’re always on the lookout for new and unusual convenience store finds in Japan, so when 7-Eleven announced it would be releasing a never-before-seen chilled soup smoothie made with grilled corn, we knew it was something we had to try.

Finding it, however, proved to be more challenging than we’d thought, as it’s currently only available at select 7-Eleven stores in Tokyo’s Chuo and Chiyoda wards. After visiting four stores in Chuo without any luck, we eventually found it at our fifth stop, where a huddle of them were lying in wait like golden treasures, gleaming at us from inside the standing freezer section.

▼ A huddle sounds like a good collective noun for smoothies.

After plucking one out and paying for it at the register, we headed over to the smoothie machine at the counter, where we scanned the barcode on the lid before tearing it off to look inside.

▼ 冷製スープ = Chilled Soup

▼ There, in the cup, we found… actual pieces of grilled corn!

The corn looked good enough to eat right away but we were here to drink it, so we popped the cup into the machine and waited for it to work its magic. With apple and banana puree also in the mix, we were curious to find out what this soup-smoothie fusion would taste like, and when it was ready, we were fascinated by the way the corn had totally disappeared and become liquid, with tiny dark grilled flecks being the only evidence of its existence.

Taking a sip, it was clear that the corn was the star of the show. Coupled with fermented rice bran, made with lactic acid bacteria and yeast for gut health, and oligosaccharides to bring out the richness and sweetness of the vegetable, the corn flavour was sweet, with a subtle smokiness, making it different to the cans of corn potage that usually come to mind when we think of a Japanese-style corn soup.

While corn potage balances sweet and savoury flavours, this variety veers towards sweetness, which is apt seeing as it’s marketed as a smoothie. In fact, as we sipped our way through the drink, we found our taste buds becoming confused over whether this should be classed as a soup or a smoothie, as the grilled vegetable component made us think we were having soup, but the overriding sweetness made us think we were drinking a smoothie.

▼ Despite the addition of fruit puree, the smoothie doesn’t taste fruity at all, making it very different from all the other fresh smoothies at 7-Eleven.

At nearly 500 yen (US$3.19), it’s also one of the most expensive smoothies in the range, and one of the hardest to find, given its very limited availability. Though there’s no word yet on whether the smoothies will expand beyond the two Tokyo wards where it’s currently being sold, this is one of the chain’s most unusual and exciting creations, and well worth trying if you’re able to find it.

As part of 7-Eleven’s latest push to explore unexpected flavour combinations and challenge our expectations of convenience store food, this is a taste odyssey we’re happy to be on, and we can’t wait to see what weird and wonderful places the chain takes us with its next new release.

title: Beautiful Totoro bonsai figure needs no watering, makes soothing rain showers whenever you want
description: Need a stress-soothing break? This figurine’s return means you can wait with Totoro while he waits for the Cat Bus. A bonsai tree can be a great way to add some picturesque tranquility to your home or work/study space. However, bonsai often require complex care routines, and if you don’t have much of a green […]
content:
Need a stress-soothing break? This figurine’s return means you can wait with Totoro while he waits for the Cat Bus.

A bonsai tree can be a great way to add some picturesque tranquility to your home or work/study space. However, bonsai often require complex care routines, and if you don’t have much of a green thumb, the hassle and stress of keeping one healthy can undo the sense of calm relaxation you were longing for.

So today let’s take a look at an alternative kind of bonsai that, in addition to being easier to care for, also has the major advantage of coming with Totoro.

Studio Ghibli specialty shop Donguri Kyowakoku has restocked its previously sold-out My Neighbor Totoro Water Garden Bonsai, which carries the subtitle of “Kasayadori.” Kasayadori refers to taking shelter from the rain, especially under the boughs of a tree, and that’s exactly what Totoro is doing in this recreation of the scene from the anime movie where he’s waiting for the Catbus to come by.

The Totoro factor isn’t the only thing that separates this from a conventional bonsai tree, either, because this figurine can make its own weather.

Drawing power from an attached USB cord, the Water Garden Bonsai functions as a desktop fountain, with rivulets pouring down around Totoro and Mei.

The clever design means that once the water falls, it gets picked up in the base of the figurine…

…and cycled back up into the upper part to fall again, so there’s no need to refill it every time you want the soothing sound of rain.

Though big sister Satsuki is absent from the scene, Mei and Totoro are joined by a friendly frog, Soot Sprites in the tree branches, and a small Totoro with a leaf for an umbrella, who wobbles as the rain falls on him.

The fountain effect can be turned on and left to run indefinitely, or set to a “voice-activated” mode that will cause rain to fall for a five-minute cycle.

▼ A video showing the fountain turned in action

Unfortunately, the other Ghibli bonsai-style water gardens shown in the video are no longer available, but the Totoro Kasayadori version, which is 22 centimeters (8.7 inches) tall and priced at 17,600 yen (US$112) is once again available for order through the Donguri Kyowakoku online store here.

title: Japanese convenience store Lawson now has stir-fried noodle-cooking robot chefs
description: Lawson expands the territory of its robo chefs as they expand their menus. You can get plenty of hot meals at convenience stores in Japan, but they usually have a cold start. Head on over to the refrigerated shelves, and you’ll find an array of pre-made bento boxes, rice bowls, and noodle sets. Pick one […]
content:
Lawson expands the territory of its robo chefs as they expand their menus.

You can get plenty of hot meals at convenience stores in Japan, but they usually have a cold start. Head on over to the refrigerated shelves, and you’ll find an array of pre-made bento boxes, rice bowls, and noodle sets. Pick one out and take it up to the register, and after you’ve paid for it, it can be heated up in the store’s microwave.

But things are different now at certain branches of Japanese convenience store Lawson, where as of this month, you can get freshly stir-fried yakisoba noodles…that are cooked by a robot.

Tokyo-based tech company TechMagic’s I-Robo 2 has actually been cooking up meals at Lawson since the summer of last year, when it started out with fried rice and mixed vegetable stir-fry. It’s since expanded its repertoire, though and now can whip up yakisoba with pork, carrots, and cabbage.

▼ Lawson’s robo-cooked yakisoba

Because the machine can cook at higher temperatures than would be safe for a human chef (it stir-fries its fried rice at over 300 degrees Celsius [572 degrees Fahrenheit], for example), the cooking process is very speedy, taking only around 90 to 150 seconds.

And to be clear, this isn’t simply reheating or finishing off an already partially cooked dish. After you place your order, either via the in-store terminal, your phone, or directly at the register, a Lawson employee loads up the robot with the necessary ingredients for what you’ve selected, then packages your meal up for you when it’s ready.

Counting all the variations (with or without pork, regular or double-sized, and with or without fried chicken as topping for the fried rice), Lawson’s robo cook can prepare a total of 13 different dishes. Prices range from 499 to 1,099 yen (US$3.29 to US$7), a little on the high end compared to pre-made convenience store fare, but not bad for something freshly cooked to order.

The first Lawson with an I-Robo 2 cook was the Kita Otsuka Icchome branch in Tokyo’s Toshima Ward. The second was the Ebina Chuo branch in the town of Ebina, Kanagawa Prefecture, whose cooking robot was installed on August 6. The Yokohama Tarumachi Sanchome (Yokohama, Kanagawa) and Koto Shiomi Icchome (Tokyo) branches will be getting theirs on August 27 and September 17, and if they prove popular, expansion to even more branches will likely follow.

title: Starbucks Japan teams up with Traveler’s Company for new stationery and goods collection

content:
Coffee and travel come together in a new range of exclusives by cult-favourite Japanese stationery brand.

For coffee lovers, every sip is a journey, with new flavours and discoveries gradually revealing themselves along the way. So when Starbucks Reserve Roastery Tokyo teamed up with Traveler’s Company, the Japanese stationery brand behind the cult-favourite Traveler’s Notebook, to create a limited-edition collection in 2019, the pairing proved to be so perfect that the two have continued releasing exclusive items together almost every year since.

▼ Making the tie-up even more special is the fact that both companies call Tokyo’s Nakameguro neighbourhood home.

This year’s collaboration between neighbours gives us five new products, based around the concept of “enjoying every day like a journey“, with designs inspired by Starbucks’ “Farm to Cup” philosophy and the Roastery Tokyo experience. All display the retro travel journal aesthetic that makes Traveler’s Company products so distinctive and popular.

▼ Starbucks Reserve Roastery Traveler’s Refill Tasting Notebook — 1,600 yen (US$11)

This special Traveler’s Notebook refill illustrates the coffee journey from farm to cup with letterpress printing and foil stamping. Inside are tasting note pages for recording coffees, meals, places visited, and memorable discoveries, allowing customers to create their own personal coffee journal.

▼ Starbucks Reserve Roastery Traveler’s Postcard Set — 2,000 yen

A set of six postcards featuring original illustrations of Roastery Tokyo icons and motifs by Traveler’s Company. Printed on a variety of textured papers, these are ideal for preserving memories of a visit or sharing handwritten messages from your travels.

▼ Starbucks Reserve Roastery Traveler’s Cotton Bag Medium — 1,800 yen

Inspired by the experience of bringing home a favourite coffee from a trip, this drawstring cotton bag is large enough to hold a bag of coffee beans, and also doubles as an organiser inside a larger bag.

▼ Starbucks Reserve Roastery Traveler’s Tote Bag — 5,000 yen

This canvas tote mimics the look of a well-travelled suitcase covered in souvenir stickers, with the Roastery Tokyo and Nakameguro being the prime destinations. Inside, you’ll find a large inner pocket that’s just the right size for holding a Traveler’s Notebook, as well as enough room to hold a tumbler or bottle, and other everyday essentials.

▼ Starbucks Reserve Roastery Traveler’s Handle Lid Stainless Steel Bottle (473 millilitres [16 ounces]) — 5,900 yen

Adorned in Roastery Tokyo-inspired travel motifs, this vacuum-insulated stainless steel bottle comes with a carry handle so you can easily carry it around with you on long journeys or even short strolls around Nakameguro.

Whether you’re a fan of Starbucks or Traveler’s Company, this is a collection that’s likely to sell out within days of its release. In a fitting twist, this range based around travel actually requires you to set out on a journey to find it, as it will be available exclusively at the Starbucks Reserve Roastery Tokyo from 6 August.
